01 / The constraint

The constraint

Predict an insurance premium from information available when a new applicant asks for a quote. A strong offline score is little use if the model needs information that arrives later.

02 / The implementation

What I built

I built the FastAPI ML microservice: typed prediction schemas, model loading from saved artifacts, preprocessing shared with training, health and readiness endpoints, SHAP feature explanations and Docker packaging. The rest of the team built the Spring Boot backend and React frontend that call it. Those parts are not my work.

03 / A deliberate choice

The tradeoff

I separated inputs available at quote time from signals available at renewal. Realised annual medical cost belongs to the latter. Histogram gradient boosting replaced random forest in the served model; SHAP exposes how features affect its predictions.

04 / Evidence, with its limits

What the work showed

The reported R² of 0.925 used realised annual medical cost, which does not exist when a new applicant receives a quote. R² measures fit against a mean-only prediction; it is not a percentage accuracy. Removing unavailable features while holding the model fixed put the quote-time result near R² 0.15. A cross-dataset audit reproduced the collapse while leaving leakage-free datasets untouched. Replacing random forest with histogram gradient boosting cut the served artifact from 95.8 MB to 0.39 MB and single-row inference from roughly 45 ms to 0.5 ms, at unchanged cross-validated accuracy. I first-authored the paper on this finding. It has been accepted at ICIDA 2026 (Springer LNNS); presentation and publication are pending.
